title: Microscopic constitutive theory of stress overshoot, yielding, and strain hardening in amorphous materials
authors: Ankit Singh, Valeriy V. Ginzburg, Alessio Zaccone
abstract: We develop a microscopic constitutive theory for the nonlinear deformation of metallic and polymer glasses based on nonaffine elasticity coupled to irreversible many-body relaxation. The theory predicts the full stress--strain response, from linear elasticity through stress overshoot and yielding to steady plastic flow. We show that stress overshoot originates from the competition between a nonaffine elastic instability induced by strain-driven loss of mechanical connectivity at the atomic/molecular level, and viscous dissipation associated with structural relaxation. For polymer glasses, finite chain extensibility naturally accounts for strain hardening at large deformation. The stretched-exponential relaxation exponent is obtained independently from stress or modulus relaxation measurements and provides the primary dynamical input to the theory. Using a small set of physically meaningful parameters, the model quantitatively reproduces experimental stress--strain curves for metallic glasses, polycarbonate, PMMA, and epoxy resins over a broad range of strain rates. These results establish a unified microscopic framework linking relaxation dynamics, yielding, plastic flow, and strain hardening in amorphous solids.
summary: This paper presents a microscopic constitutive theory to explain the nonlinear mechanical behavior of amorphous solids like metallic and polymer glasses. It successfully models the sequence from elastic loading through stress overshoot, yielding, and strain hardening by coupling nonaffine elasticity instability with structural relaxation dynamics. The results provide a unified theoretical framework validated against multiple experimental materials.
main_problem: Developing a microscopic constitutive theory for the nonlinear deformation of amorphous materials, specifically addressing stress overshoot, yielding, and strain hardening.
main_result: The model successfully reproduces the full stress-strain response across various glasses by unifying nonaffine elasticity instability with viscous structural relaxation dynamics. This establishes a unified framework linking these complex mechanical phenomena in amorphous solids.
method: The theory couples nonaffine elasticity (derived from free energy considerations) to irreversible many-body relaxation processes, modeling the total stress as a sum of elastic, viscous, and hardening components.
model_or_system: The study focuses on metallic and polymer glasses (e.g., polycarbonate, PMMA). The theory uses concepts like nonaffine displacements, strain-dependent coordination number, and stretched exponential relaxation forms to describe mechanical response.
key_observables: Stress-strain response curve, stress overshoot magnitude, yielding point, steady plastic flow regime, and strain hardening behavior.
important_parameters: Elastic modulus (E), viscosity ($\eta$), structural relaxation time ($	au_c$), viscous relaxation time ($	au_v$), and the stretched exponential exponent ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The total stress is assumed to be a linear sum of elastic, viscous, and hardening contributions. For polymers, finite chain extensibility is incorporated.
figures_summary: Figures compare theoretical predictions (solid lines) with experimental data (symbols) for MG, PC, and PMMA across various strain rates and temperatures, illustrating the characteristic sequence from loading to flow/hardening.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by defining components of stress ($\sigma_{el}, \sigma_{visc}, \sigma_{hard}$), deriving constitutive equations based on nonaffine elasticity and relaxation dynamics, and then applying these models to quantitatively reproduce experimental data for multiple amorphous materials across different deformation regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter mechanics, the underlying mathematical framework involving complex relaxation functions (stretched exponentials) and coupling between structural disorder (nonaffine effects) and macroscopic response shares conceptual links with modeling glassy dynamics in quantum or many-body systems.
